t: Early embryology, the placenta and twinning
sub: From fertilization in the ampulla to a working placenta: how the embryo is built, fed and dated, and how twins divide.

pretest.q: Where in the female tract does fertilization normally take place?
pretest.why: The oocyte is swept into the tube and meets capacitated sperm in the ampulla, the widest part of the tube. The zygote then takes about five days to reach the uterus, where the blastocyst implants.

w.Uterine fundus: The upper uterine wall is where the blastocyst usually implants around day 6, several days after fertilization has already happened higher up.
w.Isthmus of the uterine tube: The isthmus is the narrow segment next to the uterus; the zygote passes through it while cleaving, but sperm meet the oocyte earlier.
w.Ovarian surface: Fertilization on the ovary is rare; the released oocyte must first be captured by the fimbriae, and an ovarian pregnancy is an unusual ectopic site.

pretest.q: Which cells secrete the hCG detected by an early pregnancy test?
pretest.why: The syncytiotrophoblast, the invading outer trophoblast layer, secretes hCG from implantation onward. hCG acts on LH receptors to keep the corpus luteum making progesterone until the placenta takes over at about 8 to 10 weeks.

w.Cytotrophoblast: The cytotrophoblast is the inner, dividing layer that supplies new cells to the syncytium; it is not the main source of the hormone.
w.Corpus luteum: The corpus luteum is the target of hCG, not its source; it answers the hormone by continuing to secrete progesterone in early pregnancy.
w.Decidua basalis: The decidua basalis is maternal endometrium under the implantation site; it forms the maternal side of the placenta but makes no hCG.

pretest.q: A monozygotic embryo splits on day 6. Which membranes will the twins have?
pretest.why: By day 6 the blastocyst has already made its trophoblast, the future chorion, so the twins must share it. The amnion forms later from the epiblast, so splitting the inner cell mass now gives each twin its own amnion.

w.Two chorions and two amnions: Separate chorions need the split to happen by about day 4, before the trophoblast has formed around a single inner cell mass.
w.One chorion and one amnion: A shared amnion means the split came after the amnion had formed, at about days 8 to 12, and it risks tangled cords.
w.Conjoined twins in one sac: Conjoined twins come from an incomplete split at about day 13 or later, once the embryonic disc has begun gastrulation.

body: How do we count the age of a pregnancy?

Two clocks run in every pregnancy. **Gestational age** counts from the first day of the **last menstrual period**, because that date is usually known, so a term birth falls at 40 weeks, or 280 days. **Fertilization age**, also called embryonic age, counts from conception, which happens about 2 weeks after the period begins, so birth falls at about 38 weeks, or 266 days. Gestational age is therefore always about 2 weeks more than embryonic age. Due dates and ultrasound reports use gestational age, while embryology texts that speak of weeks 3 to 8 use embryonic age.
What happens in the first three weeks?

Fertilization happens in the **ampulla** of the uterine tube. Sperm must first complete {{rp4_cap|capacitation}} in the female tract; the **acrosome reaction** then digests a path through the zona pellucida, and once one sperm fuses, the **cortical reaction** hardens the zona against a second sperm. The oocyte finishes meiosis II and the two pronuclei merge. Cleavage divides the zygote without growth into a morula by about day 3, and fluid opens a cavity to make a blastocyst by about day 5.

The blastocyst has two parts with two fates: the **inner cell mass** becomes the embryo, and the outer trophoblast becomes the fetal part of the placenta. After hatching from the zona, the blastocyst begins implantation in the posterior uterine wall at about day 6. The trophoblast splits into an inner, dividing cytotrophoblast and an outer {{rp4_syn|syncytiotrophoblast}} that erodes the endometrium and secretes **hCG**, so a blood test turns positive about 1 week after fertilization. Week 2 follows a rule of 2s: a **bilaminar** disc of epiblast and hypoblast, two cavities (the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac) and two trophoblast layers.

Week 3 follows a rule of 3s. In **gastrulation**, epiblast cells move through the primitive streak to form a **trilaminar** disc, so ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm all come from the epiblast. The notochord forms in the midline and induces the overlying ectoderm to become the neural plate. Primitive streak cells that persist can form a sacrococcygeal teratoma, the most common newborn tumor, with tissue from all three layers. Weeks 3 to 8 are the embryonic period of **organogenesis**, when organ primordia form and teratogens do the most damage.
Timing decides what a teratogen does

Before week 3 the embryo is a small ball of interchangeable cells, so an exposure is **all-or-none**: enough cell loss ends the pregnancy, and anything less is repaired without a birth defect. From weeks 3 to 8 each organ is forming, so the same exposure causes structural malformations. After week 8 the fetal period brings growth, so damage shows as growth restriction or lost function.
From ovulated oocyte to implanted blastocyst, in order
Uterine and tubal secretions strip cholesterol and surface proteins from the sperm membrane, which lets sperm bind the zona pellucida.
The acrosome releases enzymes that digest a path through the zona pellucida, so one sperm can reach the oocyte membrane.
Cortical granules harden the zona to block polyspermy, and the oocyte completes meiosis II to form the female pronucleus.
The zygote divides without growing into a morula by day 3, then fluid opens a cavity to form the blastocyst by day 5.
The blastocyst sheds the zona and implants at about day 6, and the syncytiotrophoblast begins secreting hCG into maternal blood.
What does each germ layer build?

Each germ layer builds a predictable set of tissues, so a defect in one layer links anomalies that look unrelated. Surface **ectoderm** forms the epidermis, lens, enamel and anterior pituitary, and neuroectoderm forms the brain, spinal cord and retina. Neural crest cells leave the folding neural tube to form peripheral ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes and the adrenal medulla. **Mesoderm** forms muscle, bone, the heart and vessels, blood, kidneys, gonads and the adrenal cortex. **Endoderm** lines the gut and airway and forms the liver, pancreas and thyroid follicular cells.

How do the membranes and the placenta form?

The **amnion** grows from the epiblast and fills with fluid that cushions the embryo, while the **yolk sac** makes the first blood cells and the primordial germ cells. The **chorion** is extraembryonic mesoderm plus both trophoblast layers, and its villi mature from primary to tertiary villi by the end of week 3, when fetal capillaries fill their cores. The allantois, a hindgut outpouching, becomes the urachus, and the vitelline duct links midgut to yolk sac. Villi facing the implantation site form the chorion frondosum, the fetal side of the placenta, anchored in the {{rp4_decbas|decidua basalis}}, the maternal side.

Maternal and fetal blood never mix; they exchange across the villus wall. Invading trophoblast remodels the **spiral arteries** into wide, low-resistance channels that pour maternal blood into the **intervillous** space around the villi. When remodeling fails, the placenta is underperfused, which underlies preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. The umbilical cord carries two **umbilical arteries**, which return deoxygenated blood from the fetal internal iliac arteries, and one umbilical vein, which brings oxygenated blood back. A single umbilical artery is a marker for fetal renal and other anomalies.
The umbilical vein carries the oxygen

Cord vessels are named for direction, not oxygen content. The umbilical arteries carry blood away from the fetus, so they carry deoxygenated blood to the placenta, and the single umbilical vein carries the most oxygenated blood in the fetus back toward the liver and heart. A question about the highest oxygen saturation in the fetal circulation wants the umbilical vein.
What do the placental hormones do?

**Human chorionic gonadotropin** from the syncytiotrophoblast acts on the LH receptor of the corpus luteum and rescues it from its usual 14-day lifespan, so it keeps making progesterone. hCG doubles about every 2 days early on and peaks at 8 to 10 weeks, when the placenta makes enough progesterone itself, the luteal-placental shift. {{rp4_hpl|Human placental lactogen}} rises with placental mass and causes maternal **insulin resistance** and lipolysis, sparing glucose for the fetus and driving gestational diabetes. The placenta makes **estriol** only from fetal adrenal DHEA-S that the fetal liver has hydroxylated, so a low estriol can signal fetal adrenal failure.
Why does removing the corpus luteum at 6 weeks end a pregnancy, when removing it at 12 weeks does not?

Progesterone keeps the decidua intact and the myometrium quiet, and early in pregnancy the corpus luteum is its only major source. hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast keeps the corpus luteum alive through its LH receptors, but the young placenta cannot yet make enough progesterone. At 6 weeks, removing the corpus luteum therefore drops progesterone abruptly, the decidua breaks down and the pregnancy is lost unless progesterone is replaced. By 8 to 10 weeks the placenta makes enough progesterone on its own, so at 12 weeks the corpus luteum is no longer needed.
What goes wrong with implantation and placentation?

Abnormal sites and depths of implantation explain three classic emergencies. An **ectopic pregnancy** implants outside the uterine cavity, most often in the ampulla, usually because tubal scarring slows transport; the trophoblast invades the thin tubal wall, and rupture causes pain and bleeding with an hCG that rises too slowly. **Placenta previa** implants in the lower uterine segment over or near the internal os, so it bleeds painlessly late in pregnancy. The **placenta accreta** spectrum follows a deficient decidua basalis, often over a cesarean scar, so villi attach to, invade or penetrate the myometrium and cannot separate after delivery.
How do twins form, and why does the day of splitting matter?

**Dizygotic** twins come from two oocytes fertilized by two sperm, so each blastocyst builds its own chorion and amnion and the twins are always dichorionic diamniotic. **Monozygotic** twins come from one zygote that splits, and what they share depends on what had already formed. A split in the first 4 days gives two chorions and two amnions. A split at days 4 to 8 divides the inner cell mass inside one trophoblast, giving one chorion and two amnions, the most common monozygotic pattern. A split at days 8 to 12 shares the amnion too, and a split after about day 13 produces conjoined twins.

A shared chorion means a shared placenta, which often contains vessels connecting the two circulations. When flow through them is unbalanced, {{rp4_ttts|twin-twin transfusion syndrome}} develops: the **donor** twin loses volume, becomes anemic and growth-restricted, and makes little urine, so it sits in oligohydramnios; the **recipient** twin gains volume, becomes polycythemic, makes excess urine and develops polyhydramnios and heart failure. Dichorionic twins have separate placental circulations and cannot develop this syndrome.
What does amniotic fluid tell you?

After about 16 weeks most amniotic fluid is fetal urine, and the fetus removes fluid by swallowing, so fluid volume reads out fetal kidneys and gut. **Oligohydramnios** follows missing urine, as in bilateral renal agenesis; the compressed fetus develops a flat face, limb deformities and fatal pulmonary hypoplasia, the **Potter sequence**. **Polyhydramnios** follows failed swallowing or absorption, as in esophageal or duodenal atresia or anencephaly, or fetal osmotic diuresis from maternal diabetes. A malformation is an intrinsic error of development, a deformation is molding by outside force, a disruption destroys normal tissue, as amniotic band syndrome does, and a sequence is one defect cascading into others.

body.q: Ultrasound shows monochorionic diamniotic twins. Which reasoning best explains when the embryo split?
o: The split came before day 4, because two amnions can form only when each twin has its own trophoblast
The split came at days 4 to 8, because the trophoblast had already formed one chorion but the amnion had not yet formed
The split came after day 13, because sharing a chorion means the embryonic disc divided incompletely
The twins are dizygotic, because two amnions mean two separately fertilized oocytes
body.why: Membranes form in a fixed order: the trophoblast, which becomes the chorion, appears by about day 4 to 5, and the amnion forms from the epiblast around day 8. A split between these two events leaves both twins inside one chorion while giving each its own amnion. An earlier split gives two chorions, a later one gives a shared amnion or conjoined twins, and dizygotic twins are always dichorionic, so a shared chorion proves one zygote.
